pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Earth's four systems interacting (geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere)

- **Standards — UK (KS2 Science working scientifically — use and develop models; report relationships):** Children model how Earth's land, water, air and living things are connected and how a change in one affects the others.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-ESS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS2-1].

- **Operational details:** This is a systems-thinking / modelling node that ties the whole domain together (high centrality). Children first NAME the four spheres — geosphere (rock/land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), biosphere (living things) — then, crucially, trace INTERACTIONS between them with concrete examples (a river/hydrosphere carving a canyon/geosphere; plants/biosphere releasing water vapour to the atmosphere; wind/atmosphere shaping dunes/geosphere). The load-bearing skill is causal modelling: change one sphere and follow the ripple to others. Use a labelled model (diagram or built system) and push children to predict knock-on effects rather than list definitions. Keep examples local and observable before global.
bestPractices: Establish the four sphere names with clear examples before tracing interactions — naming precedes modelling.
Centre the lesson on INTERACTIONS with concrete cause-and-effect examples (river erodes rock; plants transpire into air), not four separate definitions.
Use a model children can perturb: change one sphere and predict/trace the effect on the others (systems ripple).
Start with local, observable interactions before scaling to global ones (volcanoes affecting climate).
Have children build/annotate their own model with labelled arrows showing the direction of each interaction.
keyRepresentations: A four-sphere Venn/overlap or node-and-arrow diagram with labelled interactions.
Example event cards (rainstorm, volcanic eruption, forest growth) traced across spheres.
A cause-and-effect ripple map: 'change X in one sphere → effects in others'.
Photographs annotated to tag which spheres are interacting in a scene.
commonMisconceptions: 'The four spheres are separate places' — not seeing them as constantly overlapping and exchanging matter/energy.
'Only living things count as an Earth system' — forgetting rock, water, and air are systems too.
'Interactions go one way' — missing that spheres affect each other reciprocally.
'The biosphere doesn't change the land or air' — underestimating living things' geological/atmospheric role.
'A change in one system stays contained' — not anticipating knock-on effects across systems.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds modelling how Earth's four systems — geosphere (rock/land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), biosphere (living things) — interact. The load-bearing skill is causal modelling: name the four spheres with concrete examples, then trace how a change in one ripples reciprocally through the others. Start with local, observable interactions before global ones, and push beyond listing definitions to predicting knock-on effects.

activities.title: Living Earth-systems board: change one thing, trace the ripple
feedback: If you listed the systems without connecting them, scaffold forward: 'and then what does the ash do to the air? and to the plants?' — don't restart from the names.
If you traced only one step, push one more: after ash reaches the air, what happens to the plants below, and which system is that?
If every arrow points one way, add a return path — e.g. plants (biosphere) release water vapour back into the atmosphere — to show interactions are reciprocal.

Check your terrarium: where did the water droplets on the lid come from, and which systems did the water pass through to get there? Remember the sealed jar is a simplified model of Earth's systems, not the whole Earth.
activities.rationale: A perturbable node-and-arrow model lets a child enact 'change one system, show the effect on others', which is the modelling objective; predicting before releasing turns it into causal reasoning rather than definition recall. The sealed terrarium gives an observable physical case of matter cycling between systems. The causal steps are plausible pathways whose magnitude depends on scale and conditions, not fixed quantitative outcomes.
sourceClaims: The four Earth systems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere) continually exchange matter and energy; a change in one causes effects in others.
learnerActions: Set up four labelled nodes — geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere — and draw directed arrows between them to show which systems can affect which.
Drop an event onto one node and, BEFORE releasing it, write down your prediction of how it will ripple to the other spheres.

Trace a volcano on the geosphere: ash and gases pump into the atmosphere → can block some sunlight and change weather → can affect rain and water (hydrosphere) → can stress plants and animals (biosphere).
Trace deforestation on the biosphere: less transpiration can dry the atmosphere, while bare soil lets water (hydrosphere) strip and erode the land (geosphere).
Take on a 'change just ONE thing' challenge: label each arrow in your chain with what is being exchanged (matter or energy) and in which direction.
Build a physical terrarium (soil, water, air, and plants sealed in a jar) as a hands-on complement, and observe over days how the water cycles between the systems.
activities.intendedInsight: The four spheres are not separate places but one connected system that continually exchanges matter and energy; a single change can cascade reciprocally through all of them.

activities.title: Tag the interaction in a real scene
feedback: If you only tagged interactions involving animals or plants, find a river-erodes-rock or wind-shapes-dune example to show physical systems act too.
If you named one sphere, ask which SECOND sphere it is exchanging with — every interaction needs at least two.
Name what is exchanged (water, sediment, gas, energy), not just the two spheres.
activities.rationale: Tagging real scenes builds naming and recognition of interactions and is intended to give a chance to surface and discuss the 'only living things cause change' and 'spheres are separate places' misconceptions. This recognition work supports but does not replace perturbing a model.
sourceClaims: The four Earth systems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere) continually exchange matter and energy; a change in one causes effects in others.
learnerActions: Study a rich landscape photo or scene and point to places where two systems meet — a river meeting rock, a tree meeting the air, waves meeting a beach.
For each spot, name the two spheres involved and state what is being exchanged, e.g. 'hydrosphere ↔ geosphere: the river carves the valley.'
Use lift-the-flap or cover-and-reveal: predict 'which two spheres?' before checking.
Find at least one physical–physical interaction (water eroding rock, wind shaping dunes) and one involving living things (plants transpiring, roots breaking rock).
activities.intendedInsight: Interactions between spheres are visible in ordinary scenes, and both physical systems and living systems actively cause change — not just living things.

activities.title: Sort, match, and sequence the systems
feedback: If you can order the chain but not say why each step follows, talk through the mechanism: what does the ash actually DO to the air?
If a sort is wrong, ask: is this made of rock, water, air, or is it alive? Some items (soil, a muddy river) touch more than one system — discuss which.
Matching shows reasoning only when you can state the exchange; naming the spheres without the link is incomplete.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching, and sequencing cleanly check both naming and interaction reasoning. These response formats verify understanding but, being selection-based, do not on their own elicit the independent model-building the standard calls for, so pair them with the board activity.
learnerActions: Categorise items and objects into geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere.
Match each event card (rainstorm, volcanic eruption, forest growth, drought) to at least two spheres it links, and notice that many events link more than two.
Sequence the steps of a cause-and-effect ripple chain into the correct order (e.g. eruption → ash in air → less sunlight reaching the ground → locally and temporarily cooler / stressed plants).
Explain aloud why each step causes the next, not just that it comes next.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the spheres and ordering a causal chain are different skills; a correct sequence must be justified by cause, not memorised order.

activities.title: 'And then what?' — reasoning out a ripple with a questioner
feedback: If you stop after one link, the questioner extends it: 'the river is muddier now — what does that do to the plants and animals in it?'
If you only name systems, you've shown you can list them; connecting a change from one into another is what shows you understand interaction.
Reward chains that loop back (a change returning to where it started) — that captures reciprocity.
activities.rationale: A Socratic questioner can elicit and extend a child's causal chain and surface whether they treat spheres as sealed boxes. It is strong for drawing out reasoning but does not itself produce the built/labelled model the standard asks children to make, so pair it with the modelling activity.
learnerActions: Pick an event (cutting down a forest, a long drought, a volcanic eruption) and explain its first effect on another sphere.
Respond to repeated 'and then what?' prompts, extending the causal chain one sphere at a time until you reach the biosphere or loop back to the start.
State, for a drought, one way it reaches living things AND one way it reaches the land.
Discuss the idea 'if a change in one system never touched the others, could we still call them connected?' and explain why scientists say they interact.
activities.intendedInsight: Tracing a change several steps across spheres, out loud, reveals whether you grasp interaction (relational) rather than merely naming systems.

constraints: Establish the four sphere names with clear examples before tracing interactions — naming precedes modelling.
Centre the work on INTERACTIONS with concrete cause-and-effect examples, not four separate definitions.
Start with local, observable interactions before scaling to global ones (e.g. volcanoes affecting climate).

Recognition tasks (scene-tagging, sorting, matching, sequencing) support naming and interaction reasoning but do not elicit independent construction of a model; include a build/annotate step where the child makes their own labelled arrows.
A questioner/persona can elicit reasoning but does not itself produce the labelled model the standard asks children to build — use it alongside, not instead of, the modelling activity.
A layer-toggle 3D globe can motivate by showing spatial overlap, but the target learning is causal interaction; keep the causal model in a form the child can perturb and annotate.
The terrarium is an approximation of Earth's systems; name what each component represents and acknowledge a sealed jar is a simplified model, not the whole Earth.

Present the ripple pathways (ash dimming sunlight and locally cooling water; deforestation drying the air; bare soil increasing erosion) as plausible qualitative effects whose size and duration depend on scale and conditions, not guaranteed quantitative outcomes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Listed sources[].claim are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Original row confidence was 'high'; this has not been independently re-established here.

Causal claims in the ripple examples (ash dims sunlight and cools nearby water; deforestation dries the atmosphere; bare soil increases erosion) are broadly consistent with Earth-systems science but are qualitative illustrations whose magnitude depends on scale and conditions.
The volcano-cools-hydrosphere step is a real but regional/temporary effect; the activity and constraints qualify it so it does not imply every eruption measurably cools all the oceans.

Activity 3 (sort/match/sequence) carries no sourceClaims because its distinctive teaching point — that selection formats check but do not build a model — is not directly supported by either source claim.

probeDeeper: Trace it one more step: after the ash is in the air, what happens to the plants below? Which system is that?
Give me an example where water changes the land — which two systems interact there?
If a change in one system never touched the others, could we still call them 'connected'? Why do scientists say they interact?
A drought means less water. Name one way that reaches living things and one way it reaches the land.
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree. The four Earth systems are connected, so a change in one spreads to the others. The eruption (geosphere) sends ash and gas into the atmosphere, which can block sunlight and change weather, affect rain and water (hydrosphere), and harm or change plants and animals (biosphere).

errorPatterns.pattern: The Earth systems are separate and don't affect each other ('rock is rock, air is air')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — trace one concrete pathway (ash → atmosphere → less sunlight → plants) step by step.
errorPatterns.distractor: I agree — the eruption only changes the rock; the other systems are separate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees the eruption stays within the geosphere.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names the spheres but gives an interaction only as a list, not a cause→effect link ('there's air and water and rocks and animals')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'and then what does the ash do to the air? and to the plants?'; don't reteach the names.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists the systems without connecting them; can't complete the pathway from one to another.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only living things (biosphere) cause change; the physical systems are just passive backdrops
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give a physical→physical example — a river eroding rock, rain filling a lake — to show physical systems act too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Credits only animals/plants with causing change, not air, water, or rock.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the systems as separate; says the eruption only affects the rock.
responseLevels.full: Traces at least one cause→effect pathway across systems (geosphere → atmosphere → biosphere/hydrosphere) and transfers to a new case (water eroding land, a drought reaching life) — explaining interaction, not just naming.
responseLevels.partial: Names the four spheres and asserts they're connected but can only list them, not trace a change from one into another.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A volcano erupts — that's the geosphere. A friend says it only changes the rock; it can't affect the air, the water, or living things because those are separate systems. Do you agree? Explain, tracing how the eruption reaches at least one other Earth system.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can name the four spheres yet still treat them as sealed boxes. Requiring them to TRACE a change from one sphere into another catches whether they grasp interaction (relational) versus mere naming (multistructural) — the heart of the modelling objective.

sources.claim: The four Earth systems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere) continually exchange matter and energy; a change in one causes effects in others.
